overview: Two surface appendages on bacterial cells, easily confused, but serving very different purposes: movement versus attachment/exchange.
genZNote: Flagella = the motor. Pili = the grappling hooks.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Long, whip-like appendages made of flagellin that rotate to propel the bacterial cell.
aspects.valueB: Short, hair-like protein appendages made of pilin, used for adhesion to surfaces or DNA transfer.

aspects.label: Primary Function
aspects.valueA: Motility — rotates like a propeller to move the cell toward or away from stimuli (chemotaxis).
aspects.valueB: Attachment to host cells/surfaces (fimbriae) or DNA transfer during conjugation (sex pilus).

aspects.label: Structure
aspects.valueA: Long helical filament connected to a basal body and hook that rotates via a proton motive force motor.
aspects.valueB: Shorter, straight, non-rotating rigid or semi-rigid rod-like structure.

aspects.label: Number per Cell and Arrangement
aspects.valueA: Variable arrangement: single (monotrichous), tufted (lophotrichous), one at each end (amphitrichous), or all over (peritrichous).
aspects.valueB: Often numerous fimbriae covering the surface, or a single specialized sex pilus for conjugation.

aspects.label: Clinical Relevance
aspects.valueA: Motility contributes to spread and colonization (e.g. Helicobacter pylori navigating stomach mucus).
aspects.valueB: Adhesive pili are key virulence factors for colonization (e.g. uropathogenic E. coli); sex pili enable spread of antibiotic resistance genes.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueB: Short, non-rotating, used for adhesion or gene transfer.
